analysis.title: The End of Optional Power: Asia's Role in the New Power Sovereignty Cycle
key_insights: Power has moved from a background input to a binding constraint. The same grid must now support reindustrialization, domestic data and compute, protection from extreme weather, and lower dependence on imported energy.

Flat developed-market power demand over two decades reflected offshoring of energy-intensive production as much as efficiency gains. US retail electricity sales peaked in 2007 and stayed roughly flat for 15 years, and EU demand is still about 10% below its 2008 level.

Three structural drivers make power demand intentional again: supply-chain security and reindustrialization, data sovereignty, and energy security. The near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz from late February 2026 reinforced the energy security driver for Asia.
Time-to-power (how long a new factory, fab or data center takes to secure reliable electricity) is becoming a location factor alongside labor cost, logistics, tax and market access.
The US leads the build-out and takes qualified equipment, turbine slots and engineering capacity first, so tightness elsewhere is likely to last longer than the market expects.

AI data centers are the fastest-growing load but not the only one. Of Goldman Sachs' 3.5% annual US demand growth forecast to 2030, data centers contribute 2.6 percentage points and homes, offices, industry and transport the rest.

Hyperscalers jump the queue because power is a small cost line for them. They take interconnection slots, transformer orders, turbine capacity and electricians, which leaves slower industrial projects waiting. This is latent demand that keeps the system tight even if AI spending slows.
Household demand is a second leg independent of AI: hotter summers raise peak load, EVs and heat pumps load local networks, and energy security keeps electrification funded politically.

Supply is slow to respond. Grid timelines (transmission about 10 years vs data centers 2-3 years), custom transformers with 2.5-4.5 year lead times, permitting, a shortage of skilled workers and concentrated materials (GOES, single US supplier Cleveland-Cliffs) all limit speed.

Equipment makers are adding capacity cautiously after the overcapacity of the 2010s. An aggressive industry-wide capacity push would be the clearest sign the cycle is maturing and is the signpost the authors watch most closely.

Users adapt with more compute per watt (800V DC racks, liquid cooling) and bring-your-own-power (gas turbines, engines, fuel cells, batteries). Both create equipment demand. BYOP is turning from a bridge into permanent backup.
Gas turbine orders reached about 100 GW in 2025, roughly double the 2005-24 average. GE Vernova expects to be mostly sold out through 2030 by the end of 2026.

Asia is both a demand region and a supply base. Morgan Stanley expects Asian power demand to grow about 5% a year to roughly 19,000 TWh by 2030, with grid spending of about US$1 trillion over 2025-30.

Asian supply strengths by country: Korea in transformers and switchgear, Japan in HVDC, gas turbines and nuclear, Taiwan in data-center power electronics and cooling, India in transformers, cables and EPC, China in batteries, solar and inverters.

The US and allies increasingly exclude Chinese equipment from core grids and pay a premium for qualified Korean, Japanese, Indian, Taiwanese and Western suppliers. Korean makers hold an estimated quarter of the US extra-high-voltage transformer market.
The authors favor the electrical backbone (grid equipment, power electronics, storage) over the more visible AI-linked names. The listed names are illustrative and explicitly not recommendations.

Stated risks: a pause in AI spending, too much new supply around 2027-28 (including Chinese suppliers winning approval in excluded markets), pushback on bills and sites, and valuations that already assume a multi-year shortage.

sector_views.rationale: Multi-year backlogs, pricing power from supply shortages and long qualification cycles. Korean and Japanese makers are qualified for Western grids.
Rising dollar content per data-center rack from high-voltage DC and liquid cooling, and storage demand from renewable intermittency and peak shaving.
Orders at about 100 GW in 2025 and bring-your-own-power demand from projects that cannot wait for grid connections.
Domestic grid upgrades, re-industrialization capex and BYOP demand.

earnings_insights: GE Vernova (Q2 2026 call, 22 July 2026): expects to be mostly sold out of gas turbine capacity through 2030 by the end of 2026, with more than half of its 2031 production slots also sold.
Goldman Sachs estimate: paying a premium for round-the-clock low-carbon power on all new data-center demand would cost hyperscalers about 3% of their 2028 EBITDA.

Goldman Sachs forecast, with more than 60% of the increase in the US.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Morgan Stanley estimate, with Asian data-center demand rising from about 310 TWh in 2025 to about 870 TWh.
Morgan Stanley estimate after projects under construction (21 GW) and available grid capacity (19 GW).

risk_factors: A pause in hyperscaler AI spending would ease queue pressure and likely de-rate the most AI-exposed stocks.

Too much new supply: capacity from Korean, Japanese, Indian, Chinese and Western makers comes online around 2027-28, and Chinese suppliers winning approval in excluded markets could push prices down faster than backlogs imply.
Pushback on bills and sites: Loudoun County, Virginia voted in September 2026 to advance a 12-month pause on new data-center applications, and large-load tariffs and state audits slow approvals.
Valuation: many grid-equipment leaders trade on multiples that assume the shortage lasts for years.
charts_described: Exhibit 1: developed-market power demand (US, EU and UK, Middle East, in TWh) flat for about 15 years, with a US rolling 60-month average y/y growth line, now turning up.

Exhibit 3: US total power demand CAGR 2025-30 of 3.5%, with front-of-meter data centers at 1.8% and behind-the-meter data centers at 0.8%, residential 0.4%, commercial ex data center 0.4%, industrial 0.4%, transportation 0.2%, other -0.4%.
Exhibit 4: US data-center power needed 2026-28 of 97 GW, less 21 GW under construction and 19 GW available grid, leaving a potential 57 GW shortfall.
Exhibit 5: illustrative time to market of about 10 years for transmission infrastructure versus about 2-3 years for data centers.
Exhibit 6: global gas turbine orders of about 100 GW in 2025 against a 2005-24 average of 52 GW.
geopolitical: Near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz from late February 2026. About a fifth of global LNG shipments normally pass through it, much of it bound for Asian buyers.
US-China rivalry over AI and supply chains. The US 2025 AI Action Plan frames AI as a race with China.
The US and its allies keep Chinese grid equipment out of core grids, while much of the rest of the world buys more from China.
Local-content rules, tariffs and cybersecurity reviews favor suppliers that localize production in customer markets.
Europe's 2022 gas crisis and the 2026 Hormuz disruption pushed governments toward electrification backed by domestic generation.

tension_points.bull_case: Transformer lead times of 2.5-4.5 years, multi-year backlogs, cautious capacity additions and a non-AI demand leg from households, industry and energy security keep the system tight beyond the current AI cycle.
tension_points.bear_case: Capacity announced by Korean, Japanese, Indian, Chinese and Western makers comes online around 2027-28, and a pause in AI spending or Chinese suppliers entering excluded markets could cut prices faster than backlogs imply. Many leaders already trade on multiples that assume a multi-year shortage.
tension_points.what_invalidates: An aggressive, industry-wide capacity push by equipment makers, which the authors call the clearest sign the cycle is maturing.

theme_stances.key_argument: Power is a binding constraint that will outlast the AI investment wave because of sovereignty-driven demand and slow supply response.
theme_stances.evidence: tightness elsewhere is likely to last longer than the market expects

theme_stances.key_argument: Korean, Japanese, Taiwanese and Indian makers qualified for Western grids hold long backlogs and pricing power.
